title: 1 Kings 22:1–12
context: After three years without war between Syria and Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah joins the king of Israel in a plan to retake Ramoth Gilead, but first asks to inquire for the LORD’s word. About four hundred prophets unanimously promise victory, and Jehoshaphat asks whether there is another prophet of the LORD, so Micaiah son of Imlah is summoned while Zedekiah acts out a sign of triumph. Both traditions read the scene as shared ground on the danger of seeking only welcome counsel, and the parallel account appears in 2 Chronicles 18.

verses.text: They continued three years without war between Syria and Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“They continued three years without war between Syria and Israel.” Arminian readers note that the pause follows Ahab’s treaty with Ben Hadad in 20:34, which a prophet had condemned (20:42).

The calm sets the stage for a decision that will test whether Ahab will listen to the LORD’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise connect the three years with the events of chapter 20, where Ahab released the king God had devoted to destruction.

Both traditions treat the verse as a narrative bridge that leads toward the fulfillment of the word spoken against Ahab.

verses.text: In the third year, Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat king of Judah comes down to the king of Israel in the third year. Arminian readers note that the two kingdoms, long at odds, are now allied (cf. 22:44).

2 Chronicles 18:1 adds that Jehoshaphat had joined in a marriage alliance with Ahab.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a godly king of Judah entering close partnership with Israel’s king, a relationship the Chronicler later presents as a problem (cf. 2 Chr 19:2).

Both traditions treat the alliance as a real choice with real consequences.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to his servants, “You know that Ramoth Gilead is ours, and we do nothing, and don’t take it out of the hand of the king of Syria?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Israel complains that Ramoth Gilead is theirs, yet they do nothing to take it back from Syria. Arminian readers note that the city had been promised back in Ben Hadad’s treaty (20:34), which seems not to have been kept.

Ahab’s grievance may be understandable, but he has not yet asked what the LORD wants.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Ramoth Gilead was a city of refuge in Gilead (Deut 4:43; Josh 20:8), part of Israel’s inheritance.

Both traditions observe that the plan begins with the king’s ambition, and the inquiry of the LORD comes only after Jehoshaphat asks for it.

verses.text: He said to Jehoshaphat, “Will you go with me to battle to Ramoth Gilead?” Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat answers, “I am as you are, my people as your people, my horses as your horses.” Arminian readers note the sweeping commitment he makes before any word from the LORD.

Loyalty to an ally is not wrong in itself, but it is given here without first seeking God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in the phrase a close identification with Ahab that the narrative will test.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: even a faithful king can commit himself too quickly to a partner whose way is not the LORD’s.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Please inquire first for the LORD’s word.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat says, “Please inquire first for the LORD’s word.” Arminian readers note that he does want God’s guidance, even though he has already promised his support.

The request shows a heart that still looks to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also commend the request, while noting that it comes after the commitment rather than before.

Both traditions agree that seeking the LORD’s word is right, and that the rest of the chapter tests whether that word will actually be heeded.

verses.text: Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said to them, “Should I go against Ramoth Gilead to battle, or should I refrain?” They said, “Go up; for the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
verses.arminianNotes:
About four hundred prophets say, “Go up; for the Lord will deliver it into the hand of the king.” Arminian readers note the unanimity, which Jehoshaphat does not find reassuring.

They speak of “the Lord,” not the covenant name “the LORD,” and they do not name which king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see prophets who tell the king what he wants to hear (cf. Jer 23:16–17).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: agreement among many voices is not the same as a true word from the LORD.

verses.text: But Jehoshaphat said, “Isn’t there here a prophet of the LORD, that we may inquire of him?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoshaphat asks, “Isn’t there here a prophet of the LORD, that we may inquire of him?” Arminian readers note his discernment: the four hundred do not satisfy him.

His question implies that the prophets have not clearly spoken as the LORD’s messengers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see godly discernment in Jehoshaphat, who senses that something is missing.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground on testing what claims to be a word from God (cf. Deut 18:21–22).

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of the LORD, Micaiah the son of Imlah; but I hate him, for he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.” Jehoshaphat said, “Don’t let the king say so.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahab admits there is one more, Micaiah son of Imlah, “but I hate him, for he does not prophesy good concerning me, but evil.” Arminian readers note that Ahab judges a prophet by whether he likes the message.

Jehoshaphat gently rebukes him: “Don’t let the king say so.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see in Ahab’s words a heart set against unwelcome truth.

Both traditions agree on the pastoral point: hating a messenger because the message is hard is a danger for every hearer, not only for kings.

verses.text: Then the king of Israel called an officer, and said, “Quickly get Micaiah the son of Imlah.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king calls an officer and says, “Quickly get Micaiah the son of Imlah.” Arminian readers note that Ahab yields to Jehoshaphat’s request, though reluctantly.

The true word is sent for, even by someone who does not want it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s providence bringing his prophet before the king despite Ahab’s dislike.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God’s word reaches Ahab, and he will be without excuse.

verses.text: Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah were sitting each on his throne, arrayed in their robes, in an open place at the entrance of the gate of Samaria; and all the prophets were prophesying before them.
verses.arminianNotes:
The two kings sit on their thrones in their robes at the gate of Samaria while all the prophets prophesy. Arminian readers note the public, royal setting, which adds pressure to conform.

The scene of earthly thrones will be set against Micaiah’s vision of the LORD’s throne (22:19).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the contrast between the two kings’ thrones and the heavenly throne Micaiah later describes.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: earthly power, however impressive, sits under the LORD’s rule.

verses.text: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made himself horns of iron, and said, “The LORD says, ‘With these you will push the Syrians, until they are consumed.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
Zedekiah son of Chenaanah makes horns of iron and, speaking in the LORD’s name, says, “With these you will push the Syrians, until they are consumed.” Arminian readers note that he invokes the LORD’s name directly.

Using the right words does not make a message true.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a dramatic sign-act that appears convincing but is not from the LORD.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: speaking in the LORD’s name carries great responsibility (cf. Deut 18:20).

verses.text: All the prophets prophesied so, saying, “Go up to Ramoth Gilead and prosper; for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.”
verses.arminianNotes:
All the prophets prophesy, “Go up to Ramoth Gilead and prosper; for the LORD will deliver it into the hand of the king.” Arminian readers note that the message now uses the divine name and repeats the promise.

The chorus grows louder but not more reliable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the pressure of a united voice urging the kings forward.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: truth is not settled by majority, and the reader is about to hear a different word.
